title: Repeat buyers by first-order month in 2017

brief.decision: A take-home task from our hiring team in the Netherlands, on a public dataset, Olist's orders from Brazilian marketplaces: of the people who placed their first delivered order in each month of 2017, what share came back for another delivered order on a later day, up to 31 August 2018. It helps us judge whether a discount on a customer's second order is worth testing. Count each person once, by customer_unique_id.

expected_output.grain: one row per month of 2017, a month with no new customer included

checkpoints.prompt: Ruben wants each 2017 month's new customers on Olist and how many of them came back. In orders, every order has its own customer_id, and customers gives each customer_id a customer_unique_id. How should the query tell that two orders came from the same person?

options.text: By customer_id in orders: it is the customer's own ID, so it is on every order that one person places.
By customer_unique_id, reached through customers: it stays the same on every order one person places.
By customer_zip_code_prefix and customer_city together, since one person orders from the same address.
By customer_id and customer_state together, since a person keeps one customer_id within one state.

checkpoints.prompt: In Olist, count only orders whose order_status is delivered, and follow each person by customer_unique_id in customers, never by customer_id, which changes with every order. A person's first delivered order is the earliest one over all of the person's orders in the data, 2016 included, by the day in order_purchase_timestamp as the data records it. How many people placed their first delivered order from 1 January to 31 December 2017? Type a whole number.
Write the query that answers Ruben's question.

In Olist, count only orders whose order_status is delivered, and follow each person by customer_unique_id in customers. Take the people whose first delivered order, the earliest over all of the person's orders in the data, was placed from 1 January to 31 December 2017, by the day in order_purchase_timestamp as the data records it. What percentage of them placed another delivered order on a later day than that first order, up to and including 31 August 2018? A second order on the same day as the first does not count. Type the percentage rounded to 2 decimals, for example 12.34.

In Ruben's table from Olist, the share of each month's new customers who placed another delivered order on a later day, up to 31 August 2018, is lower for the months late in 2017, with November and December the lowest. Nothing else has been checked yet. Ruben asks: does this show that the customers won late in 2017 are less loyal?

options.text: Yes. A lower share means fewer of those customers ever ordered again, so the customers won late in 2017 were less loyal.
Not from this table. Each month is counted up to 31 August 2018, so later months had less time to come back; compare them over equal windows.
No. November held a large sale, and people who buy in a sale never come back, so the low shares only show the one-time buyers of that one big sale.
No. The late months have more new customers, and a larger group always shows a smaller share, so the months cannot be compared at all.

checkpoints.prompt: Write 2 to 4 sentences for Ruben: how the share of new customers who came back moved across 2017, the share for the whole year, one caveat about the comparison, and one next step.

model_plan:
Metric formula: per cohort month, cohort_customers counts the people whose first delivered order was placed in that month; repeat_customers counts those of them with another delivered order on a later day, up to and including 31 August 2018; repeat_pct is 100 times repeat_customers divided by cohort_customers, rounded to 2 decimals, and missing for a month with no new customer.
Output grain: one row per month of 2017, a month with no new customer included.
Tables and keys: orders joined to customers on customer_id for customer_unique_id; a step at one row per person with the day of the first delivered order; a list of the twelve months of 2017, with the people joined to it by LEFT JOIN on the cohort month.
Filters: only delivered orders, for the first order and for the later one; first delivered orders from 1 January 2017 up to, not including, 1 January 2018; later orders on a later day and no later than 31 August 2018.
Edge cases: customer_id changes with every order, so it never shows a return; a first order that was canceled or never delivered does not set the month; a second delivered order on the first day is not a return; a person whose first delivered order was in 2016 is in no 2017 month; a month with no new customer shows 0, 0 and a missing share.
Expected row count: 12
model_answer_template: Of the {CP2} people who placed their first delivered order on Olist in 2017, {CP4} percent came back for another delivered order on a later day by 31 August 2018, and the share is lowest for the months late in the year. A second-order discount would therefore reach a large group of one-time buyers, but the late months had less time to come back, so their low shares do not yet show weaker loyalty. Next, I would compare every month over the same window, such as the 180 days after the first order, and then test the discount on one month's new buyers against a group without it.
follow_up_question: How do the months compare when each is counted over the same 180 days after the first order?

data_source.label: Real data: Olist's Brazilian e-commerce orders, about 100,000 orders made at several marketplaces in Brazil from 2016 to 2018, without the geolocation file. Source: Olist, on Kaggle. Licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
